lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eAl \u003cb\u003ebajar:
"

Going down a group the atomic radius increases (more shells) and the ionization energy decreases; going across a period the radius decreases and the ionization energy increases (greater effective nuclear charge). These two trends explain almost all of descriptive chemistry: reactive metals are at the left and bottom, reactive nonmetals at the right and top.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eCon la capa de valenc:
"

With a complete valence shell (ns²np⁶) the noble gases are monatomic and inert. Only the heaviest ones (Kr, Xe, Rn), with lower ionization energy, form compounds with very electronegative elements (XeF₂, XeF₄, XeO₃, KrF₂). Their boiling points increase downward (He 4 K; Xe 165 K) because of polarizability.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEl \u003cb\u003egrupo:
"

Group 2 forms M²⁺ cations. They are less reactive than the alkali metals: Be does not react with water, Mg does with steam, and Ca, Sr and Ba react with cold water. The hydroxides are increasingly basic and soluble (Mg(OH)₂ sparingly soluble; Ba(OH)₂ soluble). Ca and Mg are essential in biology (bones, chlorophyll, enzymes).

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEl carácter ácido–bas:
"

The acid–base character of the oxides changes across a period: the oxides of metals (Na₂O, MgO) are basic and form hydroxides; Al₂O₃ is amphoteric; those of nonmetals (SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₃, Cl₂O₇) are acidic and form oxoacids. The pH of the aqueous solution of each oxide drops from ≈ 14 to ≈ 0.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eLos \u003cb\u003ehaló:
"

The halogens (X₂) are diatomic; the state changes because of increasing London forces: F₂ and Cl₂ gases, Br₂ liquid, I₂ solid. The oxidizing power follows F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂ (E° = 2.87; 1.36; 1.07; 0.54 V): a halogen displaces the ion of another one lower down (Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂).

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eLos metales del \u003:
"

The metals of group 1 have a single s¹ e⁻ that they lose easily (low I₁): they are very strong reducing agents, soft, of low density. They react with water: M + H₂O → MOH + ½H₂, ever more violently toward Cs. They are stored under oil. The ions give flame colors (Li red, Na yellow, K lilac).

"
